sceneHappening: How to live to please God, and a word of hope for those who have lost loved ones
summary: Finally, brothers, Paul urges and exhorts them in the Lord Jesus that, as they received from him how they must walk and please God, they should abound more and more. They know what instructions he gave them through the Lord Jesus. "For this is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to possess himself of his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of lust, even as the Gentiles who don't know God; that no one should take advantage of and wrong a brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as also we forewarned you and testified. For God didn't call us for uncleanness, but in sanctification. Therefore he who rejects this doesn't reject man, but God, who has also given his Holy Spirit to you." About brotherly love they have no need for anyone to write, for they themselves are taught by God to love one another, and they do this toward all the brothers in all Macedonia; but Paul urges them to abound more and more, and to "aspire to lead a quiet life, and to mind your own business, and to work with your hands, even as we instructed you; that you may walk properly toward those who are outside, and may have need of nothing." Then, concerning those who have fallen asleep: "We don't want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who are asleep, so that you don't grieve, even as the rest, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus. For this we tell you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left to the coming of the Lord, will in no way precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God. The dead in Christ will rise first, then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air. So we will be with the Lord forever. Therefore comfort one another with these words."
whySettingMatters: Chapter 4 turns from memory and prayer to instruction. The call to "abstain from sexual immorality" must be read against the background of a port city where sex was part of religious worship and commerce and was generally unrestrained; Paul's ban was radical. The phrase "possess his own vessel" (skeuos) in 4:4 can mean control his own body or acquire (or live with) his own wife, and translators and commentators are divided. The words about "mind your own business" and "work with your hands" fit a church in which some may have stopped working because they expected the Lord to return soon (see 5:14 and 2 Thessalonians 3:6-12). The passage on those who "have fallen asleep" (4:13-18) answers a real worry: believers had died since Paul left, and the Thessalonians feared they had missed out on the Lord's return. Paul's answer is that the dead in Christ will rise first and that all will be with the Lord. The word translated "meet" (apantēsis) was used for a delegation going out to welcome a visiting official and escorting him into the city, which fits the picture of believers going out to meet the Lord and coming with him. How this passage fits with the rest of the New Testament's teaching on the end, including the idea of a "rapture" and its timing, has long been debated by Christians; the passage itself is about comfort, and ends with "comfort one another with these words."

people.note: Urges holy living and comforts the grieving.
Learning to please God and grieve with hope.
Who will descend from heaven with a shout.
Whose passion and lust the believers must not imitate.

questions: Paul says holiness is "the will of God." What do the practical examples (sex, work, love) tell you about what holiness looks like?
He says "aspire to live quietly... work with your hands." Why might ordinary, unglamorous living be a goal?
Paul doesn't say believers shouldn't grieve, only not to grieve "as those who have no hope." What does hope change about grief?
The passage ends with "comfort one another with these words." How would you use it that way?
